lit.\u0027\u003cdiv class=\"calc-step\"\u003:
"
2 · What reaction to expect
"
lit.\u0027\u003cp class=\"muted small\"\u003:
"

With NaOH (pKa of H₂O = 15.7) simple carbonyls enolize only to a small extent; it is enough for the aldol to occur with aldehydes, but not with esters.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eAl calentar, la base:
"

On heating, the base removes the α H of the aldol (enolate) and the pair expels the OH⁻ from the β carbon (E1cB mechanism): but-2-enal (crotonaldehyde) forms, a conjugated α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compound. The C=C–C=O conjugation stabilizes it and the loss of water makes the process irreversible: this is the aldol condensation.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eCon \u003cb\u003eNaOH:
"

With NaOH/EtONa there is an equilibrium between carbonyl and enolate (K = 10pKa(HB) − pKa(HA)): the enolate can react with its own carbonyl (aldol). With a strong, non-nucleophilic base (LDA, NaH) the carbonyl is converted completely into the enolate before the electrophile is added: this allows directed crossed aldols and alkylations. Change the precursor and the base in “Lab” and look at the value of K in “Calculation”.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl \u003cb\u003ebenza:
"

Benzaldehyde has no α H: it cannot form an enolate, it only acts as an electrophile. Propanone forms the enolate and attacks benzaldehyde; after dehydration 4-phenylbut-3-en-2-one (benzalacetone) is obtained, conjugated with the ring and the ketone. This avoids the mixture of four products that would appear on combining two enolizable carbonyls.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl alcóxido capta un:
"

The alkoxide picks up an H⁺ from the solvent (water or alcohol) and 3-hydroxybutanal is obtained, an aldol (aldehyde + alcohol): an OH group at the β position relative to the C=O. At low temperature and with dilute base the reaction stops here and is reversible (retro-aldol).

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl carbono nucleófilo:
"

The nucleophilic carbon of the enolate (C=C π pair, arrow 1) attacks the electrophilic carbon of a second ethanal molecule; the π bond of the C=O moves onto the oxygen (arrow 2). An alkoxide with a new C–C bond forms: two 2-carbon molecules give one 4-carbon molecule. It is the same attack along the Bürgi–Dunitz trajectory as in addition to the carbonyl.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eLa base toma el H α (:
"

The base takes the α H (arrow 1), the pair of the C–H bond forms the C=C double bond (arrow 2) and the π bond of the C=O moves onto the oxygen (arrow 3). The enolate is a hybrid of two resonance forms: C⁻ (carbanion) and O⁻ (vinyl alkoxide). It is a nucleophile at C and therefore forms C–C bonds. With NaOH only a small fraction of the ketone is converted to enolate; with LDA the conversion is complete.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eLos hidrógenos del \u:
"

The hydrogens on the α carbon (the neighbor of the carbonyl) are acidic: pKa ≈ 17 (aldehyde), 19–20 (ketone), 25 (ester), compared with 50 for an alkane. The reason: when H⁺ is lost the negative charge is delocalized onto the oxygen. If the C–H lies between two carbonyls (malonate 13, acetoacetate 10.7, acetylacetone 8.9) the acidity grows even more.

"
